title: Citicorp and Travelers become Citigroup
what: The merger of Citicorp, owner of Citibank, and Travelers Group, owner of the Travelers insurance business and the brokerage Salomon Smith Barney, was completed on 8 October, creating Citigroup, the world's largest financial services company. John Reed of Citicorp and Sanford Weill of Travelers run it together as co-chairmen and co-chief executives. Combining a bank with an insurer breaks the Depression-era Glass-Steagall rules; the Federal Reserve has granted a temporary waiver, and the company expects Congress to change the law. Salomon closed its bond arbitrage desk in July and was among the firms that put money into the rescue of the hedge fund Long-Term Capital Management in September.
why: Listing beat: one-stop shopping for banking, insurance and investments, launched in the middle of the 1998 market crisis. The bet on a change in the law paid off within a year.

title: Congress nears repeal of the wall between banks and Wall Street
what: House and Senate negotiators are working out the final version of a law that would repeal the parts of the 1933 Glass-Steagall Act separating banks, securities firms and insurers. Democrats have agreed to support it after Republicans strengthened lending rules for poor neighbourhoods and added privacy protections. For Citigroup, which was formed in 1998 on a temporary waiver, the law would make its structure permanent. Its shares rose 23% in October.
why: The market priced in the law before it passed; the connection to the October move is likely rather than proven (Citigroup's own announcements for the month were not checked).

title: Citigroup buys Mexico's Banamex for $12.5 billion
what: Citigroup agreed to buy Banamex, one of Mexico's largest banks, for $12.5 billion. In February it agreed to buy European American Bank in New York for $1.9 billion.
why: Banamex made Citigroup a leading bank in Mexico; Citigroup decided in 2022 to exit consumer banking there and was still selling Banamex in 2025.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citigroup (read 2026-10-03, citing New York Times, 18 May 2001)

title: Citigroup's star analyst questioned over WorldCom
what: WorldCom, whose shares and bonds Citigroup's Salomon Smith Barney helped sell and whose deals it advised on, has collapsed into bankruptcy after admitting a $3.8 billion fraud. Salomon's telecom analyst Jack Grubman, who recommended WorldCom shares until April, told Congress he saw no warning signs. New York's attorney general Eliot Spitzer is investigating conflicts of interest among Wall Street analysts, Salomon among them, and Citigroup faces lawsuits over its role in Enron's financing.
why: The reputational bill for the boom: the banks that sold Enron and WorldCom to investors paid billions in settlements over the next three years. Citigroup's shares fell 13% in July, more than the market.

title: Citigroup's profit holds up; bank shares rally
what: Citigroup reported on 15 October that core income rose 17% to $3.79 billion in the third quarter, with record results in its consumer business. Stocks rallied from the lows they hit early in the month, and Citigroup's shares rose a quarter in October.
why: The relief rally after the scandal summer; the S&P 500 rose 9% in the month and banks more. (Time check: 'their lows of the bear market' assumed the bottom was in.)

title: Citigroup settles research probe, sets aside $1.3 billion
what: Citigroup reached a settlement in principle with the SEC, the stock exchanges and New York's attorney general over its analysts' research, the allocation of shares in hot share offerings and related practices. It is taking a fourth-quarter charge of $1.5 billion after tax, most of it a $1.3 billion addition to reserves for the settlement and for lawsuits over Enron and research.
why: The first instalment. The final settlement in April 2003 cost $400 million in penalties and funding for independent research; WorldCom and Enron cost far more.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/831001/000095012302012169/y67237exv99w1.txt (Citigroup press release, 23 December 2002; read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/831001/000095012303004835/y85900exv99w1.txt (28 April 2003; read 2026-10-03)

title: Chuck Prince to succeed Sandy Weill
what: Sanford Weill announced that Charles Prince, head of the corporate and investment bank, will become chief executive by 1 January 2004, with Robert Willumstad as chief operating officer; Weill stays chairman until the 2006 annual meeting. Citigroup also settled with the SEC, bank regulators and the Manhattan district attorney over its Enron dealings, paying $145 million.
why: Weill's empire passed to Prince, who was chief executive when the mortgage bets were made.

title: Citigroup pays $2.65 billion over WorldCom
what: Citigroup agreed to pay $2.65 billion before tax ($1.64 billion after tax) to settle the class action of WorldCom investors over the shares and bonds it sold for the company. It is taking an after-tax charge of $4.95 billion in the second quarter, which also covers its remaining exposure to Enron and other litigation.
why: One of the largest securities settlements ever; Citigroup still earned a record $17 billion in 2004.

title: Citigroup pays $2 billion to settle Enron suit
what: Citigroup agreed to pay $2.0 billion to settle the class action by Enron investors, who accused the banks of helping Enron hide its debts. Earlier this year it settled claims over Global Crossing for $75 million.
why: The end of the boom-era bills; from 2005 the risks Citigroup was taking were in the mortgage market.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/831001/000095012305007233/y09884exv99w1.txt (Citigroup press release, 10 June 2005; read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/831001/000095012305002524/y06392exv99w1.txt (2 March 2005; read 2026-10-03)

title: Citigroup to cut 17,000 jobs
what: Citigroup announced on 11 April that it will eliminate about 17,000 jobs, some 5% of its workforce, in a restructuring meant to cut costs and lift its long-lagging share price.
why: The shares had gone nowhere for years under Prince; pressure to grow helped push the bank deeper into mortgage securities.

title: 'As long as the music is playing, you've got to get up and dance'
what: Asked whether Citigroup would keep financing leveraged buyouts despite worries about credit markets, chief executive Charles Prince said: 'As long as the music is playing, you've got to get up and dance. We're still dancing.'
why: The most quoted line of the crisis; Citigroup's shares fell 9% in July and the music stopped within weeks.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chuck_Prince (read 2026-10-03, citing New York Times DealBook, 10 July 2007)

title: Citigroup warns of a 60% profit drop on mortgage losses
what: Citigroup warned on 1 October that dislocations in mortgage and credit markets would cut its third-quarter profit by about 60%, and on 15 October reported net income of $2.4 billion. On 31 October an analyst at CIBC, Meredith Whitney, said Citigroup was paying out more in dividends than it earned and might need to raise about $30 billion or cut its dividend.
why: The first hit, and the first public analysis that the bank was short of capital; it set up November's collapse.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/831001/000110465907072200/a07-24989_1ex99d1.htm (Citigroup press release, 1 October 2007; read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/831001/000110465907074791/a07-26588_1ex99d1.htm (15 October 2007; read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citigroup (read 2026-10-03)

title: Prince quits as Citigroup warns of up to $11 billion in write-downs
what: On 4 November Citigroup said the value of its $55 billion of subprime mortgage exposure, most of it in the top-rated slices of complex securities called CDOs, had fallen by $8-11 billion since September; Charles Prince resigned, with Robert Rubin as chairman and Sir Win Bischoff as acting chief executive. Citigroup said it had no plans to cut its dividend. On 26 November it sold $7.5 billion of securities convertible into shares to the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority. The shares fell 21% in the month.
why: The 'super senior' securities had been treated as nearly riskless; now they were the hole. The dividend promise lasted two months.

title: Citigroup loses $9.8 billion and cuts its dividend
what: Citigroup, led since December by new chief executive Vikram Pandit, reported a fourth-quarter net loss of $9.83 billion after $18.1 billion of write-downs and credit costs on subprime exposures, cut its dividend, and raised $12.5 billion in a private sale of convertible preferred shares to long-term investors, plus about $2 billion more in the market. With the Abu Dhabi deal it has raised almost $30 billion in two months.
why: The first of five straight quarterly losses. Raising capital from sovereign funds at falling prices diluted shareholders again and again.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/831001/000110465908002661/a08-1961_1ex99d1.htm (Citigroup press release, 15 January 2008; read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/831001/000110465908002663/a08-1948_1ex99d1.htm (read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/831001/000114420408003260/v100398_ex99-1.htm (22 January 2008; read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/831001/000114420407066977/v096976_ex99-1.htm (read 2026-10-03)

title: Government rescues Citigroup
what: On 17 November Citigroup announced about 52,000 more job cuts, and its market value fell to about $20 billion from $244 billion two years earlier. On 23 November the Treasury, the Federal Reserve and the FDIC agreed to guarantee losses on $306 billion of Citigroup's loans and securities and to invest a further $20 billion. In return the government gets preferred shares and warrants, a say in pay and lending, and the dividend is cut to a cent a share.
why: The largest bank rescue of the crisis. The shares fell 39% in November despite it: shareholders were being kept alive, not made whole.

title: Citigroup loses $8.3 billion and splits itself in two
what: Citigroup agreed on 13 January to merge its Smith Barney brokerage into a joint venture controlled by Morgan Stanley. On 16 January it reported a fourth-quarter loss of $8.29 billion and said it would reorganise into Citicorp, its core bank, and Citi Holdings, a collection of businesses and troubled assets to be sold or run down. The shares fell 47% in January.
why: The end of the financial supermarket: the model built by Weill was being dismantled in public.

title: Government to take up to 36% of Citigroup
what: Citigroup announced on 27 February that it will swap preferred shares held by the government and private investors for common shares, which could give the U.S. government a stake of up to 36% and raise tangible common equity to as much as $81 billion. Existing shareholders will be heavily diluted. It also took a further $9.6 billion goodwill write-down for 2008. The shares fell 58% in February.
why: The low point. Shareholders were not wiped out, but their share of the bank was cut to a fraction.

title: Pandit: Citigroup is profitable again
what: In a memo to employees released on 10 March, chief executive Vikram Pandit said Citigroup was profitable in January and February, with its best quarter-to-date performance since the third quarter of 2007 and revenues of $19 billion excluding write-downs. Bank shares rallied from their lows, and Citigroup's rose 69% in March.
why: The turn. The memo marked the bottom for Citigroup and, near enough, for the whole market.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/831001/000095012309004333/y75154exv99w1.htm (letter to employees, 9 March 2009, filed 10 March; read 2026-10-03)

title: Share swap done; government owns a third; Citi out of the Dow
what: Citigroup completed its exchange of preferred shares for common shares in late July, leaving the U.S. government with about a third of the company. It reported second-quarter net income of $4.3 billion, thanks to a $6.7 billion gain on the sale of Smith Barney. In June it was dropped from the Dow Jones Industrial Average because of the government's stake.
why: The new capital structure that the August rally was built on; existing holders owned a much smaller slice of a safer bank.

title: Citigroup repays $20 billion of rescue money with a record share sale
what: Citigroup agreed with the government to repay $20 billion of rescue money and end the loss-sharing guarantee, and sold $17 billion of new shares plus $3.5 billion of other equity to pay for it, the largest share offering in U.S. history. The sale cuts the Treasury's stake to about 27%; it agreed not to sell for 90 days. The shares fell 19% in December.
why: Freedom from the government's pay limits, paid for by more dilution.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/831001/000095012309070361/y80976exv99w1.htm (Citigroup press release, 14 December 2009; read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/831001/000095012309071395/y81063exv99w1.htm (16 December 2009; read 2026-10-03); https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citigroup (read 2026-10-03)

title: Treasury sells its last Citigroup shares, at a profit
what: The U.S. Treasury sold its remaining 27% stake in Citigroup, ending government ownership; taxpayers made an overall profit of about $12 billion on the rescue. Citigroup has been profitable in each of the first three quarters of 2010.
why: The rescue repaid in full. The share price was still about 90% below its 2007 level.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citigroup (read 2026-10-03, citing Reuters and Washington Post, 7 December 2010); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/831001/000110465911001741/a11-4145_1ex99d1.htm (read 2026-10-03)

title: Citigroup completes a 1-for-10 reverse split
what: Citigroup combined every ten of its shares into one, effective after trading on 6 May; the shares trade on a split-adjusted basis from 9 May. A shareholder's stake is unchanged: ten times fewer shares, each worth ten times more. Citigroup plans to reinstate a quarterly dividend of 1 cent a share now that the split is done. It earned $10.6 billion in 2010.
why: The game's price series is adjusted for the split, so the chart shows no jump; news quoted before May 2011 uses prices one tenth of the game's. The split was the formal close of the rescue era.
source: https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/831001/000119312511131957/dex991.htm (Citigroup press release, 9 May 2011; read 2026-10-03); https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/831001/000114420411016019/v215370_ex99-1.htm (21 March 2011; read 2026-10-03)

title: Citigroup's profit rises to $3.8 billion
what: Citigroup reported third-quarter net income of $3.8 billion, up from $2.2 billion a year earlier, although $1.9 billion of it came from an accounting gain on the fall in the value of its own debt. Credit losses fell 41%. After two months of steep losses, bank shares recovered, and Citigroup's rose 23% in October.
why: The shares had fallen 19% in August and 17% in September; October's rally came with the market (+11%).

title: Citigroup fails the Fed's stress test
what: The Federal Reserve rejected Citigroup's plan to return capital to shareholders after its annual stress test, citing the bank's planned payouts and the risks in its international loans.
why: A sign that regulators did not trust Citigroup's numbers or controls; the issue came back in 2014 and in 2020.
source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Citigroup (read 2026-10-03, citing CBS News, Huffington Post and MarketWatch, March 2012)

title: Vikram Pandit out; Michael Corbat takes over
what: Vikram Pandit stepped down as chief executive on 16 October, the day after reporting third-quarter results, and the board elected Michael Corbat to succeed him. Chairman Michael O'Neill praised Pandit for guiding Citigroup through the crisis.
why: A board-led change after the stress-test failure; Corbat's job was to make the bank simpler and pass the regulators' tests.

title: Fraud at Banamex; Citigroup fails the stress test again
what: Citigroup disclosed a $235 million after-tax loss from a fraud at Banamex, its Mexican bank, discovered in February, and cut its 2013 results. On 26 March the Federal Reserve again rejected its capital plan, this time on concerns about the quality of its risk management.
why: Recurring weak controls, the theme that led to the 2020 regulatory orders.

title: Citigroup passes the Fed's stress test
what: The Federal Reserve did not object to Citigroup's capital plan this year, after rejecting it in 2012 and 2014, so the bank may raise its dividend and buy back shares. Two of the 31 banks tested had their plans rejected on qualitative grounds.
why: The start of the payout years; passing again in 2016 let Citigroup return more than $10 billion a year to shareholders.

title: Citigroup returned $10.7 billion to shareholders in 2016
what: Citigroup reported fourth-quarter net income of $3.6 billion and said it returned $10.7 billion to shareholders in 2016 through dividends and share buybacks, buying back 196 million shares. In April 2016 it announced it would wind up Citi Holdings, its 'bad bank'.
why: The payout years: passing the stress tests in 2015 and 2016 let Citigroup buy back shares cheaply below book value.

title: Citigroup's profit beats the gloom
what: Citigroup reported fourth-quarter 2018 net income of $4.3 billion excluding a tax item and said it returned $18.4 billion to shareholders in 2018. After a 9% fall in the S&P 500 in December, stocks rebounded, and Citigroup's shares rose 24% in January.
why: A rebound after a 20% fall in December 2018; the market rose 8% in January.

title: Regulators order Citigroup to fix 'longstanding deficiencies'
what: The Federal Reserve ordered Citigroup on 7 October to correct longstanding deficiencies in its risk management, data quality and internal controls, and its bank regulator fined it $400 million. In August Citibank had mistakenly wired $900 million to lenders of the cosmetics company Revlon. Jane Fraser, named in September, will succeed Michael Corbat as chief executive in February 2021, the first woman to lead one of the four biggest U.S. banks.
why: The orders hung over Citigroup for years, limiting its growth and forcing a costly overhaul of its systems.

title: Citigroup discloses its exposure to Russia
what: After Russia invaded Ukraine and was cut off from the SWIFT payment system, Citigroup disclosed billions of dollars of exposure to Russia, where it owns a bank, AO Citibank. Its shares fell 10% in March, after 9% in February.
why: Citigroup was the most international U.S. bank and so the most exposed; only in late 2025 did it put the Russian bank up for sale, booking a $1.2 billion loss. Wikipedia and its Reuters source give different exposure figures, so the amount is left out.

title: Fraser reorganises Citigroup around five businesses
what: Citigroup announced on 13 September the biggest overhaul of its structure in decades: the heads of its five businesses (Services, Markets, Banking, Wealth and U.S. Personal Banking) will report directly to chief executive Jane Fraser, and layers of regional management are being removed.
why: The simplification investors had asked for since 2008; job cuts followed.

title: Citigroup loses $1.8 billion and plans 20,000 job cuts
what: Citigroup reported a fourth-quarter net loss of $1.8 billion, after a $1.7 billion payment to the deposit insurance fund, $1.3 billion of reserves for Russia and Argentina, Argentina's devaluation and a $780 million restructuring charge; it earned $9.2 billion for 2023. It plans to cut about 20,000 jobs.
why: The cost of the clean-up, taken in one quarter; the shares rose anyway as investors looked through it.

title: Citigroup agrees to sell a quarter of Banamex
what: Citigroup reported third-quarter net income of $3.8 billion, up from $3.2 billion, and said it has agreed to sell a 25% stake in its Mexican bank Banamex, a step toward selling it entirely; it took a $726 million goodwill charge on the deal. It returned $12 billion to shareholders in the first nine months. The shares are around $100, the highest since the autumn of 2008.
why: The long recovery made visible; the price was still far below the pre-crisis peak, and the share count much higher.

title: Citigroup's profit jumps 42%
what: Citigroup reported first-quarter revenue up 14% and net income up 42%, with banking fees up 12% in a record first quarter for mergers and Markets revenue above $7 billion. Chair and chief executive Jane Fraser called it an exceptionally strong start to 2026. The shares rose 13% in April as the market climbed 10%.
why: Earnings finally matching the turnaround story; the market rally did much of the rest.
